publisher_summary: Parkinson’s disease begins years before motor symptoms appear. Longitudinal blood transcriptomics shows that DNA repair and stress response pathways are most altered during this prodromal phase, then lose discriminative power in established disease. In this Comment, we link these changes to aging-related DNA damage and consider their biomarker potential. Mirroring aging hallmarks, they suggest a prodromal intervention window, when mechanisms driving dopaminergic neuron vulnerability are most active and potentially tractable.

title: Bidirectional regulation between brain angiotensin and MFG-E8 pathways modulates resolution of neuroinflammation in aging
abstract: Aging is characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation, to which overactivation of the brain angiotensin II (Ang II)/AT1 receptor (AT1R) axis significantly contributes. Milk fat globule–EGF factor 8 (MFG-E8, lactadherin) promotes microglial efferocytosis and resolution of inflammation, but its interaction with AT1R signaling, particularly in the aging brain, remains unclear. We identify a bidirectional regulatory loop between Ang II/AT1R and MFG-E8/αvβ3 integrin pathways using neuronal–glial models and young and aged human and mouse brain tissue. Ang II/AT1R activation reduced MFG-E8 expression and impaired clearance of apoptotic neurons. Conversely, apoptotic signals and recombinant MFG-E8 suppressed AT1R expression and inflammatory signaling while enhancing pro-resolving pathways, involving NF-κB and STAT3 modulation. Aged brain tissue showed AT1R overactivation associated with reduced MFG-E8 expression. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized feedback interaction that limits resolution of neuroinflammation during aging, identifying the Ang II–MFG-E8 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Validation and refinement of a biomarker panel for frailty assessment and prediction of muscle weakness in older adults
abstract: Frailty is a complex geriatric syndrome characterized by age-related declines in physiological function and cognitive reserve. To promote early prevention and intervention, minimally invasive and objective biomarkers that can detect frailty progression are required. We aimed to identify biomarkers associated with frailty progression and to elucidate their relevance to the Japanese version of the Cardiovascular Health Study (J-CHS) criteria, consist of five components (unintentional weight loss, self-reported exhaustion, muscle weakness, slow walking speed, and low physical activity). A total of 168 individuals (61 robust, 25 pre-frail, and 82 frail) enrolled in the NCGG (National Center for Geriatrics and Gerontology) Biobank were analyzed. Clinical information, blood-test data, aging-related factors, and gene-expression data were integrated for the analysis. First, linear regression identified one clinical factor, five aging-related factors, and 251 gene-expression factors associated with frailty. Subsequent logistic regression analyses examining each J-CHS components highlighted six candidate biomarkers. Cross-validation further suggested that three of these biomarkers—SMI, apelin, and GDF15—may represent potential biomarkers. Finally, retrospective and prospective analyses further demonstrated that those biomarkers were predictive of future muscle weakness, yielding a concordance index of 0.70. In conclusion, we validated and refined a biomarker panel consisting of SMI, apelin, and GDF15 that is associated with frailty, particularly muscle weakness (a major J-CHS component). These biomarkers may be useful for frailty assessment. Longitudinal analyses further suggested that they may be associated with the future development of muscle weakness in initially robust older adults, although validation in larger prospective cohorts is warranted.
